newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says Russia-NATO pact could end bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says Russia-NATO pact could end bloodshed.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Monday he believed the NATO-Russia pact agreed last week could bring an end to the "heartache and bloodshed" that have marked European history over the last 200 years.

Speaking to reporters before a White House meeting with North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) Secretary General Javier Solana, Clinton was seeking to blunt criticism of the pact, announced last Wednesday.
"We have had a long Cold War, and two world wars in the 20th century, and a 19th century full of heartache and bloodshed because people were arguing over territory in Europe," Clinton said.

"We now have a chance to create a European continent where nation states for the first time say they are going to respect each others' borders and work together on common security problems," he added.

"To find a framework which accomplishes that and which also keeps the United States ... tied to the security and the freedom and the territorial integrity of Europe is an extraordinary achievement and it gives us a chance to write a whole new chapter in the 21st century," he said.
NATO and Russia agreed last week to sign a partnership agreement that appeared to ease Moscow's fears about the alliance's eastward expansion.
To be signed in Paris on May 27, the accord will pave the way for NATO's expected invitation to Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic to join the alliance, which Russia has fought tooth and nail.
The accord has come under criticism from some in the United States who argue the Clinton administration has given Russia too much of a say in the alliance's business.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin last week said the deal would be binding on the Western alliance and that it would give Moscow the means to block any decision by NATO it did not approve of.
In contrast, Clinton last week said that under the pact: "Russia will work closely with NATO but not in NATO, giving Russia a voice in but not a veto over NATO's business."

The seeming contradiction is explained by the fact that the accord creates a new NATO-Russia Permanent Joint Council, with monthly meetings by ambassadors and twice-yearly gatherings of foreign and defence ministers.

U.S. officials said Russia would have a veto power within that council but stressed that the North Atlantic Council -- made up of the 16 current NATO members -- will continue to set alliance policy and would not be subject to any Russian veto.
